newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta's deficit nearly three times forecast.
newsitem.headline: Malta's deficit nearly three times forecast.

text.p: Malta's government deficit soared to nine percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in 1996 instead of a projected 3.2 percent, Finance Minister Lino Spiteri said on Monday.
Presenting the first budget of the new Labour government, he said the government planned to reduce the deficit to just over six percent this year and would reduce it further in 1998.

Spiteri said the government was projecting revenue of Lm514.7 million ($1.39 billion) and expenditure of Lm615.9 million this year compared to an actual revenue of Lm446.1 and expenditure of Lm578.8 in 1996.

He told parliament the difference between ordinary revenue and expenditure had "exploded" to Lm132.8 million ($358.5 million) from a projected Lm54 million, and Malta ended 1996 with a deficit of Lm108.8 million from the projected Lm32.8 million.
At the end of 1997, the deficit after considering grants from other countries is projected to be Lm82.2 million, he said.
Spiteri said GDP rose by four percent in real terms in the first nine months of 1996 to reach Lm884.3 million. Both exports and imports were down, the former more than the latter.
Unemployment rose to 3.7 percent in September 1996 from 3.4 percent in September of the previous year.
Inflation was 2.94 percent for the year ending September 1996, slightly down from the previous comparative period, he said.
Spiteri did not announce an expected alternative system to Value Added Tax, introduced by the previous Nationalist government in 1995. That government was defeated in last October's general election.
The Labour government, the minister said, would stick to its electoral promise to repeal the tax, but it would be issuing a white paper for consultation on its proposals.
As a first step, however, a tax on hotel and catering services for tourists was being cut to five from 10 percent.
Spiteri said the government in the coming year would insist on a reduction in tax evasion and exercise better control over its spending.

Income tax would not be touched but a series of indirect taxes would be introduced to lift revenue. They range from a higher car registration tax to higher excise duties on cigarettes. The taxes were such as not to harm economic activity, he said.
Postal rates are to go up some 10 percent and ordinary petrol would increase to 30 cents a litre from 26.4 cents, with unleaded going to 27.5 cents from 25.3 cents. ($1 = Lm0.36)
